steps.ask: To test injectivity, what do you assume about $f(a)$ and $f(b)$? What must you then show?
steps.title: Test injectivity: assume equal outputs

lines.text: $f$ is injective if $f(a) = f(b)$ forces $a = b$.
Equal outputs force equal inputs, so $f$ is injective.

steps.ask: Which values must $f$ be able to reach? Write $f(x) = y$ for one of them. What do you do next?
steps.title: Test surjectivity: solve f(x) = y

lines.text: $f$ is surjective if every $\hl{1}{y}$ in the codomain $\mathbb{R}$ equals $f(x)$ for some $x$ in the domain.
This $x$ is a real number for every real $\hl{1}{y}$, so every $\hl{1}{y}$ is reached and $f$ is surjective.

steps.ask: If $f$ passes both tests, what kind of function is it?
steps.title: Classify

lines.text: $f$ is both injective and surjective, so it is bijective.

problems.note: A quadratic instead of a linear function, so the curve is not one-to-one: the injectivity test now looks for two inputs with the same output. The surjectivity test completes the square to find the smallest output. The classification step is the same.

legend.1: the codomain value tested for surjectivity

steps.ask: Would a quadratic pass the same algebra test as the linear function? Try two different inputs and compare their outputs. Which pair would you choose?
steps.title: Test injectivity: look for two inputs with the same output

lines.text: Two different inputs, $0$ and $6$, give the same output, so $g$ is not injective.

steps.ask: What form of $x^2 - 6x + 5$ would show the smallest value $g(x)$ can take? Rewrite it in that form.
steps.title: Test surjectivity: find the smallest output

lines.text: Since $(x - 3)^2 \ge 0$, every output satisfies $g(x) \ge -4$. Test a value below $-4$, such as $\hl{1}{-5}$.

steps.ask: Can $g(x)$ ever equal $-5$? Use the form you found to decide.
steps.title: Try to solve g(x) = -5

lines.text: A square cannot be negative, so there is no real $x$ with $g(x) = \hl{1}{-5}$. Then $\hl{1}{-5}$ is in the codomain but is never reached, so $g$ is not surjective.

steps.ask: Does $g$ pass either test? What does that mean for bijective?
steps.title: Classify

lines.text: $g$ is neither injective nor surjective, so it is not bijective.

problems.final: \hl{2}{g \text{ is neither injective nor surjective, so not bijective}}

problems.note: Compared with the previous problem, the domain and codomain are finite sets rather than all real numbers, so there is no algebra or curve and the outputs are listed one by one. The surjectivity test now checks for a missing element of the codomain, and the classification step is the same.

legend.1: the codomain value tested for surjectivity

steps.ask: Which inputs are in the domain? Work out $h$ for each one and list the outputs.
steps.title: Work out every output

steps.ask: Are any two of your outputs the same? What does that tell you about injectivity?
steps.title: Test injectivity

lines.text: The outputs $2, 3, 4$ are all different, so different inputs give different outputs and $h$ is injective.

steps.ask: Does every element of the codomain appear as an output? Which input would have to give the one that is missing?
steps.title: Test surjectivity

lines.text: The codomain is $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$. The element $\hl{1}{1}$ is not an output, because $x + 1 = \hl{1}{1}$ gives $x = 0$, which is not in the domain. So $h$ is not surjective.

steps.ask: Which of the two tests did $h$ pass? Does a bijection need both?
steps.title: Classify

lines.text: $h$ is injective but not surjective, so it is not bijective. (A bijection needs the same number of elements in the domain and codomain: here $3 \ne 4$.)

problems.final: \hl{2}{h \text{ is injective, not surjective, so not bijective}}
